body.x: A car's infotainment screen, its driver-assistance functions and its vehicle controls do not carry the same safety requirements, yet as carmakers move from many separate electronic control units (ECUs) to centralized and zonal electrical and electronic (E/E) architectures, more of these functions have to share the same computing hardware. Keeping them from interfering with one another is a software problem.
What if a single processor could run several operating systems side by side, each isolated from the rest?

That is the job of the automotive hypervisor from PERSEUS Co., Ltd., a system software company founded in 2016 and based in Siheung, Gyeonggi Province. Led by CEO Sangbeom Seo, the company says it specializes in foundational software for software-defined vehicle (SDV) architectures. Its PEGASUS Hypervisor was selected as a Grand Innovation Award winner in the Future Mobility category of the FIX 2026 Innovation Awards, and the company will exhibit at DIFA 2026, which its application describes as a gathering of key technologies and business trends in future mobility, to present its technologies.

PERSEUS lists a portfolio that includes the PEGASUS automotive hypervisor, the AEGIS security virtualization solution, the TACHYON Linux fast-boot solution, and MCU security solutions including GAIA and AEGIS-let. According to the company, PEGASUS is a Type-1 hypervisor that lets multiple operating systems and vehicle functions run securely and independently on a shared automotive processor. It supports both CPU and MCU architectures and has achieved ISO 26262 ASIL-D functional safety certification for both, the company says, and it supports a wide range of automotive processors and operating systems for centralized and zonal E/E architectures.

The exhibition will include hardware-based demonstrations. The first is what PERSEUS describes as the first public demonstration in Korea of PEGASUS running on an NVIDIA Thor SoC platform. Using an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor board, PEGASUS runs five virtual machines (VMs) at once, one L4T Linux GUI VM and four Linux CLI VMs. Visitors can watch each VM operate independently on the same SoC through real-time network and process activity shown on the GUI and terminals. PERSEUS says the demonstration illustrates how a user-facing GUI environment and vehicle backend services can be separated and run on one computing platform, pointing toward architectures that consolidate digital cockpit, autonomous driving and vehicle control functions.

The second demonstration is in an automotive MCU environment. One setup runs six real-time operating systems at the same time and shows how a software fault in one VM can be isolated and recovered from without affecting other workloads. A separate resource-management demonstration shows how system performance changes with the CPU core allocation for each VM. A Performance Monitor tracks the status of the hypervisor and each VM, and a Configuration Manager handles the setup and management of virtualized environments. The company says together they show how several vehicle functions can be consolidated on shared hardware while keeping functional independence, system stability and efficient use of computing resources.

The third is TACHYON. PERSEUS says it will demonstrate the Linux fast-boot technology reducing the startup preparation time of a rear-camera application from about 15 seconds to 1.5 seconds. The company says it is designed for in-vehicle applications, such as rear-view cameras, that need to work as soon as the vehicle starts, and that developers can keep their existing Linux-based environment.

The company says its aim at the show is to present these technologies directly to the Korean automotive and mobility industries, including domestic automakers, Tier-1 and Tier-2 suppliers, semiconductor companies, research institutions and technology partners. It plans to discuss customers' challenges in system integration, functional safety, cybersecurity, boot performance and efficient use of hardware resources during the move to SDVs, and to explore how its technology fits customers' specific E/E architectures and development environments, with a view to proof-of-concept (PoC) projects, joint development and later production use. PERSEUS says it will also reflect feedback gathered at the show in future product and business development.

On its track record, PERSEUS says it has carried out hypervisor development contracts and PoC projects with global automakers, Tier-1 suppliers and semiconductor companies, and that some are progressing toward production applications. It says details of individual customers and projects, including specific export countries and automaker names, are not disclosed because of confidentiality agreements, and are shared only where those agreements allow. The company works with semiconductor partners including Arm, NXP, Renesas and Infineon, and has carried out joint research with Fraunhofer IESE in Germany on functional-safety verification for automotive software. It is also expanding business and technology cooperation through exhibitions such as Automotive World in Japan and ongoing technical meetings.

PERSEUS says it is currently working on hypervisor and foundational software projects with automakers, Tier-1 suppliers and semiconductor companies, mainly in Europe and Asia. Its overseas business includes software licensing, customer-specific software development and technical collaboration on SDV architectures. The company regards the U.S., Japan and Europe as its key markets, citing active U.S. work in advanced automotive computing, autonomous driving, AI and SDV development, and the shift toward centralized and zonal E/E architectures in Japan and Europe. It says that with PEGASUS covering both CPU and MCU architectures, it aims to build long-term partnerships that run from early E/E architecture discussions and PoCs to joint development and production.

The company also names challenges. Automotive foundational software has to be validated against each customer's E/E architecture, semiconductor platform, operating system and functional safety requirements, so the path from technical evaluation and PoC to production adoption can take a relatively long cycle. Strict confidentiality in projects with global automakers and Tier-1 suppliers can limit public use of customer references. Overseas expansion also requires close technical communication, continuous customer support and strong local industry networks, and PERSEUS says it is strengthening customer engagement through international exhibitions, technical meetings, and collaboration with semiconductor companies and research institutions.

Its plan is to expand PoC and joint-development projects with automakers, Tier-1 suppliers and semiconductor companies in the U.S., Japan and Europe, with the goal of moving them into a production software licensing business centered on PEGASUS. PERSEUS says it will keep extending its virtualization technology from CPU to MCU environments to support next-generation SDV E/E architectures, including central computers and zone controllers, and will look for new customers and partners at automotive exhibitions and technical events in the U.S. and elsewhere. In the medium to long term, it aims to grow software licensing revenue linked to vehicle production volumes and to take its virtualization, functional safety and security technologies beyond automotive into other embedded industries.

Now in its third year, FIX 2026 (Future Innovation Technology Expo) is a future-industry exhibition that brings together and links innovative technologies in future mobility, robotics, AI and ICT, and startups. It runs from Wednesday, Oct. 21, to Saturday, Oct. 24, at EXCO in Daegu. Under the theme "AI, Beyond Tech into Reality," the exhibition shares industry trends and core technologies through AI-based technology exhibitions, conferences and lectures by Korean and international experts, and networking programs.
